paragraphs.text: Before turning to its immediate policy decision, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) discussed key economic developments and its judgements around them, as well as its views on monetary policy strategy. The latest data and analysis underpinning these topics were set out in the accompanying November 2026 Monetary Policy Report .

The impact of protracted conflicts overseas on global energy prices remained the main source of uncertainty for the UK inflation outlook. The path for inflation was being shaped by the scale and duration of the energy and other global supply shocks, their knock-on impact on medium-term inflation through potential indirect and second-round effects, and the outlook for domestic activity and spare capacity. Monetary policy could not influence global energy prices, but was being set to ensure that the economic adjustment to them occurred in a way that achieved the 2% inflation target sustainably. The Committee would particularly need to guard against second-round effects that created inflation persistence, while considering any trade-off with weakness in economic activity.

Energy prices had remained sensitive to geopolitical news, and there had been significant further rises in spot and futures prices. The front-month Brent crude oil futures contract and the UK front-month natural gas futures contract averaged $108 per barrel and 216 pence per therm, respectively, over the 15 UK working days ending 27 October. These were 38% and 81% higher than at the time of the July Monetary Policy Report, and 5% and 27% above the respective 2026 Q4 futures-price assumptions in the July Report adverse scenario. Although a credible and sustained de-escalation of the conflict in the Middle East could lead prices to fall, continued periodic conflict, wider regional escalation or further damage to refining capacity could lead to persistently higher prices than embodied in current futures curves. There had also been a drawdown in energy supply buffers during 2026 which could amplify price pressures.

In the September UK CPI inflation outturn of 3.5%, direct energy effects had contributed around 1 percentage point, most of which was driven by fuels. These direct energy contributions were projected to build further in the next few quarters but then fall back, reflecting base effects and conditioning assumptions for wholesale energy prices based on futures curves that were downward sloping. There had been little sign so far of indirect effects from higher energy prices on other consumer goods prices, and in particular food inflation had remained lower than expected earlier in the year. Members discussed whether this was a sign of either diminished, or simply delayed, indirect effects. Although many firms were already facing higher prices for oil and refined products, some had not yet seen large rises in gas or electricity prices owing to hedging or longer-term fixed-price contracts. Agency intelligence suggested that many firms were also absorbing higher costs partly through lower profit margins.

The outlook for indirect effects on inflation would depend on the duration of the energy shock, and the extent to which firms could bear down on other costs or rebuild their margins in a stronger demand environment. The Committee judged that, for the most part, firms’ buffers would only prove temporary and that these cost pressures could eventually pass through into higher consumer prices if the energy shock persisted. There was, however, a risk that firms’ resilience to the energy shock would not last, instead resulting in weaker demand and then limiting firms’ pricing power.

The latest near-term inflation projection by Bank staff, which was based on energy prices averaged over the 15 UK working days to 27 October, was for headline CPI inflation to reach around 4½% in 2027 Q1, around 1¼ percentage points higher than at the time of the July Report, and around 5% in 2027 Q2.

Members noted that there was still limited evidence to date of second-round effects in wage and price-setting, although such effects typically only emerged with a longer lag and few indicators could yet be expected to reflect the impact of recent increases in energy prices. Forward-looking indicators of wage and price expectations from the DMP survey and Agents’ intelligence had moved little since September, though households and firms’ attentiveness was judged to be high, and there was a risk that outturns for wage settlements would turn out higher than firms’ current expectations if they were faced by outturns for headline inflation in the new year that were stronger than they had previously anticipated. Since second-round effects were likely to be state-dependent and the outlook for headline inflation had risen materially, the Committee judged that the risk of material second-round effects emerging had risen further since September and could remain a risk for some time.

The Committee continued to monitor wider global cost pressures, such as those triggered by adverse weather events and demand for AI components, although the potential impact of these risks on UK inflation was likely to be much smaller than for the energy shock and was not judged to have increased significantly since September. Despite the energy shock and these non-energy cost pressures, global activity growth had proved more resilient than expected, although it was expected to fall back next year.

The Committee had been briefed on the Budget on 28 October. The projections and scenarios in the November Report were conditioned on announced Government policy. The new policy measures in the Budget were expected to have a downward impact of ¼ percentage points on CPI inflation by 2027 Q2 and a small impact on activity. In absolute terms, the stance of fiscal policy remained likely to detract from growth over the medium term.

The Committee discussed the recent path of domestic activity and its implications for inflationary pressures. Since September, there had been further evidence of the resilience of activity despite higher energy prices. Momentum had been provided by the impact of global growth on UK exports, and some positive impact from the deployment of artificial intelligence. The impact of artificial intelligence on the UK economy was uncertain but was likely to affect both demand and supply. There was also some evidence that consumer demand had held up so far despite the impact of higher energy prices on real incomes, although the most recent consumer confidence reading suggested that this might not be maintained.

There was uncertainty around the extent to which the recent strength in GDP growth might persist, but on balance members judged that it was likely to fall back somewhat in the coming quarters. The outlook for growth would be sensitive to the behaviour of households and firms in the face of rises in energy costs and tighter financial conditions.

The increase in growth had been associated with signs of a stabilisation of the margin of slack in the economy, although members continued to differ in their views on how wide that margin was in absolute terms. It was likely that some slack would persist given the headwinds facing demand from households and firms. It would also be important to judge whether the factors boosting productivity growth over the past two years would lead to an ongoing boost to potential growth in the economy and, more broadly, the extent to which future growth would reduce spare capacity in the economy.

The Committee discussed the extent to which the underlying disinflation process that had been underway for some time before the Middle East conflict had proceeded as expected. Many measures of underlying inflation were no longer falling, and were judged to be somewhat above rates consistent with meeting the inflation target in the medium term. For some members, the news on domestic activity and underlying inflation was a signal that monetary policy had not been as restrictive as previously judged. For other members, it was premature to draw too much signal from outturns over the past few months, given the volatility of short-term economic indicators, uncertainty about the impact of technological change, and the difficulty of interpreting measures of underlying inflation completely independently of the energy shock.

Forward market interest rates had remained elevated compared with pre-conflict levels, and had continued to feed through to rates faced by some households and firms. Benchmark two-year mortgage rates had risen by nearly 50 basis points since the beginning of September. According to the Bank’s latest Market Participants Survey, the median expected path for Bank Rate had increased since September, reaching 4% in November and 4.25% in February, but had remained below the UK short-term interest rate curve.

Most members judged that the stance of monetary policy was still restrictive, although this judgement was sensitive to the choice of measure of the monetary stance, for example the extent to which it reflected expected inflation. The stance of monetary policy would also be experienced differently by different households and firms depending on their exposure to higher energy prices, technological change and interest rates. Members also noted that growth rates of lending to businesses had remained strong, although new mortgage approvals for households had been falling.

The Committee considered the updated central projection and the two scenarios that were set out in the November Report. The central projection assumed that there would be greater second-round effects on wage and price-setting than in the July Report owing to higher energy prices. The adverse scenario explored the risk of persistently higher energy prices and an additional mechanism for larger second-round effects which might occur as a consequence. The weaker demand scenario assumed that the recent resilience of domestic growth would falter and that widening spare capacity in the economy would limit the scope for second-round effects to emerge. These scenarios would all require different monetary policy responses if any of them were to materialise.

Taken together, the Committee judged that the risk of stronger inflationary pressure had increased further since the September meeting. While most members continued to judge that there was still a margin of slack in the economy and that policy was still restrictive, it was less clear that this would impart sufficient disinflationary pressure to bring inflation back to target in a timely manner, given the further upward pressures on inflation which were anticipated and that had increased the forward-looking risks to inflation persistence. This could be especially important since households and firms appeared more attentive to outturns for headline inflation than in the past. While financial conditions had tightened materially compared with the start of the conflict, a rise in Bank Rate at this meeting would support the broader transmission of tighter financial conditions.

Given the significant uncertainty around the geopolitical situation and the impact of tighter financial conditions so far, the Committee would continue to keep the cumulative evidence on the propagation of the energy shock through the UK economy under close review, and judge whether the level of Bank Rate was imparting sufficient restrictiveness. Most importantly, the Committee would continue to monitor the prospects for second-round effects in price and wage-setting by considering the evolution of pay, pricing behaviour and slack via the available data and surveys, consistent with the framework set out in Box A in the November Report.

Eight members (Andrew Bailey, Sarah Breeden, Swati Dhingra, Megan Greene, Clare Lombardelli, Huw Pill, Dave Ramsden and Alan Taylor) preferred a 0.25 percentage point increase in Bank Rate at this meeting. The duration and scale of the energy price increase had generated sufficient inflationary pressures in the pipeline to warrant an increase in Bank Rate. There was a range of views among these members about the extent to which the underlying disinflationary process prior to the conflict had continued, the degree of spare capacity in the economy, and the restrictiveness of the current monetary policy stance. These members agreed that, although evidence of second-round effects had been limited, the availability of evidence would increase over time, and would continue to need close monitoring, along with the implications of developments in energy prices for medium-term inflationary risks.

Catherine L Mann preferred a 0.5 percentage point increase in Bank Rate at this meeting. From a risk management and credibility perspective, an activist approach was needed to prevent persistent inflationary dynamics becoming embedded as the economy reached thresholds that threatened to cause non-linear responses in price and wage-setting.
The Chair invited the Committee to vote on the proposition that:
Bank Rate should be increased by 0.25 percentage points, to 4% .

Eight members (Andrew Bailey, Sarah Breeden, Swati Dhingra, Megan Greene, Clare Lombardelli, Huw Pill, Dave Ramsden and Alan Taylor) voted in favour of the proposition. Catherine L Mann voted against the proposition, preferring to increase Bank Rate by 0.5 percentage points, to 4.25%.

sections.heading: Votes to increase Bank rate by 0.25 percentage points, to 4%.

paragraphs.text: Andrew Bailey : There has been a material further increase in energy prices. UK economic activity has strengthened and the labour market appears to be stabilising (Box C). Domestic services price inflation has flattened off. Meanwhile, indirect and second-round effects have not emerged yet (Box A). Firms are cutting costs and their margins are being compressed, while they are also benefiting from longer fixed-price energy contracts and cost hedging mechanisms. To varying degrees, these approaches can only be temporary. The central projection and weaker demand scenario require an alleviation of the factors that have pushed up energy prices to validate the slope of energy futures curves. Put simply, it requires real progress towards settling the conflict in the Middle East. Absent this, risks to energy prices, and so to inflation, are to the upside. In view of the news, the case is clear for a 25-basis point rise now. Without news which softens the risks to inflationary pressures, I can see the argument for a further increase in rates and thereafter taking a more conditional approach, dependent on the evidence on energy prices and inflation dynamics. Recognising that some of the upward slope in the curve is explained by risk premia and not expected rates, the current level of restrictiveness is broadly appropriate.

Sarah Breeden : Increased energy prices have further materially raised the near-term inflation outlook. Activity and the labour market have been more resilient than expected, but slack remains (Box C). Consistent with this and firm intelligence, little evidence has emerged so far of material second-round effects and indirect pass-through has been weaker than expected. While some measures of domestic inflation have flattened, I do not yet conclude that the earlier disinflation has stalled, given overlapping energy shocks and the seasonal pattern of wage negotiations. Slack will be leaning against the risk of material second-round effects (Box A). But with inflation expected to be above the threshold for non-linear effects, and little sign of a rapid or durable resolution to the conflict, the degree of inflationary pressure in the pipeline is now sufficient to warrant an increase in Bank Rate. The longer energy prices remain high the more likely persistent inflationary effects take hold, which would require further tightening in Bank Rate. But this will also depend on how energy prices propagate, especially given the risk that demand weakens. I will continue to assess the balance of risks at each meeting. For now, I judge the current restrictiveness of financial conditions as sufficient to balance these.

Swati Dhingra : Even as underlying inflation normalised in line with peer countries, previous votes to maintain Bank Rate in restrictive territory guarded against immediate inflation risks from the unfolding energy shock. The scale and persistence of the rise in wholesale energy prices imply that households and businesses will continue to face higher energy costs in the near term. Broad-based price pressures remain subdued, however, and we cannot yet distinguish between delayed pass-through and weaker pass-through on the evidence available (Box A). Growth has been firmer than anticipated (Box C), partly reflecting an AI-driven sectoral and investment boost that presents two-sided risks to the inflation outlook. Set against this, the combined drag from energy prices and higher mortgage rates continues to weigh on real disposable incomes, limiting consumption growth and weakening activity in consumer-facing services. Raising Bank Rate by 25 basis points provides additional insurance against upside risks from stronger pass-through and firmer growth in demand. To support maintaining Bank Rate at a higher level for an extended period, I would need to see clear evidence of a recovery in firms’ pricing power and households’ purchasing power alongside signs of mutually reinforcing wage and price pressures.

Megan Greene : Since September, we have had a more prolonged shock, a further leg up in energy prices and there is evidence of less benign initial conditions when the shock hit. Evidence of second-round effects has remained scant as expected, but the risks have clearly shifted to the upside. Underlying services inflation has been flat since spring and underlying wage growth is stuck around 3.5%, above target-consistent levels. GDP growth has surprised to the upside and aggregate credit volumes remain stronger than expected. Staff analysis shows we may have been marginally in a low inflation, loose labour market regime when the Iran conflict emerged, but we’ve since entered a high inflation, loose labour market regime. We project inflation will remain above the threshold in which expectations are more sensitive to outturns for most of the outlook period, likely buoying pay settlements in 2027 and 2028. I believe the output gap is smaller than we think and has likely peaked. We continue to face Knightian uncertainty, but a rate hike now is appropriate based on the central outlook rather than just risk management considerations. Additional hikes will likely be required going forward, though further out this will depend on pay, pricing behaviour and slack.

Clare Lombardelli : The conflict has lasted longer than expected. This has kept oil, gas and refined product prices elevated, making the inflationary effects of the energy shock larger and more persistent. Cost pressures have remained elevated for sufficiently long that there is now a greater risk of second-round effects becoming embedded in price and wage-setting (Box A). Despite this, economic activity appears more resilient than previously expected (Box C). And recent data suggest that underlying disinflation may have stalled. There are some downside risks to the outlook for inflation, either from a more benign path for energy prices or a slowdown in economic activity. But overall I view the balance of risks to the inflation path as upside to our forecast given the ongoing energy price uncertainty and limited evidence of slack. Current circumstances warrant a 25-basis point increase in Bank Rate at this meeting. In the absence of evidence of weaker inflation pressures, there is likely to be a case for a further increase in rates in the near term. Beyond that, the path for rates is conditional on the interaction of the underlying economy, higher energy prices, the nature of their transmission and any further shocks.

Huw Pill : Raising Bank Rate by 25 basis points at this meeting represents a significant step towards attaining the monetary policy stance needed to address current threats to price stability, including those stemming from uncertainty surrounding events in the Middle East and their influence over energy prices in the medium term. That uncertainty and its impact remains potentially considerable and of indeterminate duration. Nonetheless, of itself, a single 25-basis point hike is unlikely to be sufficient. Achieving the level of Bank Rate necessary to confront challenges and risks to lasting achievement of the 2% inflation target is likely to require more policy tightening, including in the near term. Looking into next year, monetary policy decisions should then become more dependent on evidence of inflation persistence and second-round effects, were it to emerge in the data flow. At each meeting, a broad-based interpretation of new data and surveys will support the extraction of the policy-relevant underlying signal from a range of indicators. Developments in domestic pay and pricing dynamics (Box A) deserve particular focus since they offer insight into the potential strength of second-round effects and, as such, inform the assessment of lasting threats to price stability.

Dave Ramsden : The outlook for inflation has deteriorated, with higher energy prices following re-escalation of the conflict since July. I have also become somewhat less confident about the domestic disinflation process, the degree of slack, and how restrictive the policy stance has been to date. Activity has proved more resilient than expected (Box C), slack in the labour market is levelling off, and private sector wage growth has stopped declining. These less favourable starting conditions increase the risk of second-round effects (Box A). Indirect effects have been smaller and slower to build than anticipated in July, but looking ahead, are projected to be larger and more protracted. Risks around the inflation outlook have shifted further to the upside. Nevertheless, households and firms’ resilience could weaken, with adjustment occurring through employment losses or business failures rather than prices. A 25-basis point increase in Bank Rate is necessary now to ensure the appropriate degree of restrictiveness. I will continue to assess the evidence at each meeting, in particular how likely high energy prices are to feed through to other prices and the economy more broadly, by monitoring the evolution of pay, pricing behaviour, and slack.

Alan Taylor : It is essential to communicate, and for markets to understand, that, as of now, this is not the start of a hiking cycle: policy isn’t on a pre-set, unconditional path. The risk is curve dislocation and unwarranted tightening in financial conditions. Rather, from an already restrictive position, this is a risk-management ‘one-for-now’ insurance hike. What has changed since July, and even September, is the magnitude of the energy disruption. A second, larger shock has roughly doubled the inflationary impulse; gas is beyond April’s worst scenario, while refined-product prices have risen sharply. The case for holding rested on avoiding such a shock and seeing no sign of second-round effects. The first condition has now failed. We lack evidence of second-round effects, but the larger shock raises the risk. That motivates insurance now. Further tightening, however, depends on continued energy price pressure (a function of stochastic geopolitics that we are ill-equipped to predict) as well as unfolding evidence of propagation into domestic wages, price-setting and expectations, particularly through the 2027 pay round. The next move could be up, down, or sideways. Telling data will arrive soon.

sections.heading: Vote to increase Bank rate by 0.5 percentage points, to 4.25%.

paragraphs.text: Catherine L Mann : My recent votes to increase Bank Rate by 25 basis points represented a ‘down payment’ to lean against second-round effects, reinforce credibility, and uphold ‘good policy’ (in the language of my Great Moderation speech). The challenge: projected CPI inflation reaches 4.9% by mid-2027 and would be some 25 basis points higher absent the measures announced at the latest Budget. This projection is conditioned on a significant decline in energy prices; similar futures curves earlier this year have not eventuated. My policy strategy importantly is informed by research, which points to non-linear inflation risks. Households are particularly attentive to energy and food price inflation, which may be reflected in 2027 wage demands. With CPI inflation at 3.5% in September, the economy has crossed the estimated statistical threshold into a high inflation-tight labour market regime where the asymmetric behavioural responses of households and firms support more robust second-round effects. A different research approach estimates that the economy may well have breached the policy credibility threshold, which worsens the policy trade-off. Moreover, a substantial inflation risk premium is in the UK yield curve, reflecting five years of above-target inflation, where it has averaged 4.7%. Therefore, from a risk management and credibility perspective, a 50-basis point hike in Bank Rate is ‘good policy’.
In line with the arrangements announced following the September MPC meeting, the stock of UK government bonds held for monetary policy purposes on 4 November was £362 billion.

sections.part: 1. Review of financial, economic and monetary developments and policy options
sections.heading: Financial market developments
paragraphs: Ms Schnabel started her presentation with the observation that, since the Governing Council’s monetary policy meeting on 22-23 July 2026, euro area financial markets had continued to be driven by energy price developments, with market attention turning to the global rise in long-term yields amid a resilient euro area macroeconomy.

Persistently high energy prices, reinforced by concerns about higher food price inflation, had pushed market expectations regarding the outlook for inflation and policy rates higher. Energy prices and futures curves had moved up owing to renewed US-Iran hostilities. In Europe, the focus had shifted from oil to refined products and gas. The price and futures curve of gas oil – a refined, diesel-type product – had moved up significantly, reflecting concerns about limited refining capacity. Similarly, European gas prices had risen to the highest level recorded since early 2023, and low European gas storage levels could put further upward pressure on gas prices. The recent heatwave in Europe and what could likely be a strong “El Niño” event had also added to concerns about upward pressure on prices, with international food prices rising significantly over recent months.

The market-based inflation outlook continued to be driven primarily by energy price developments. Over time, markets had reassessed the persistence of the inflation shock. Following the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East, markets had quickly priced in a substantial near-term inflation shock, with the December 2026 inflation fixings jumping sharply. The June 2027 inflation fixings had responded less strongly initially but had risen steadily since mid-April as market participants increasingly viewed the conflict as a persistent source of disruption. As a result, markets currently expected inflationary pressures to extend well beyond the initial energy price impulse. Looking further ahead, the December 2027 inflation fixings had so far increased only modestly, suggesting a decline in inflation during 2027, in line with the staff projections, while remaining above 2%.

This reassessment had been reflected in expectations for the ECB’s terminal rate, which had risen above 3% for the first time during this hiking cycle. Markets were fully pricing in a rate hike at the present meeting and had priced in 84 basis points of hikes overall by the end of 2027, compared with 64 basis points at the time of the July meeting. Respondents to the Survey of Monetary Analysts took a more benign view, with the median expectation suggesting only a final rate hike at the September meeting. In the United States, monetary policy expectations also pointed to a somewhat higher terminal rate, with markets currently pricing in between one and two rate hikes in 2026.

Market discussion had focused on the global rise in long-term yields, which had originated in the United States where high private and public issuance, concerns about the fiscal trajectory and uncertainty about inflation had pushed yields higher. Since the Governing Council’s July monetary policy meeting, the nominal overnight index swap (OIS) yield curve in the euro area had shifted higher in a broadly parallel manner. The move in the front end had been primarily driven by higher inflation compensation and higher expected rates, reflecting the expected monetary policy response to the inflation shock. The longer end – the five-year rate in five years’ time – had been driven by higher real term premia, which likely reflected more duration to be absorbed by markets due to increased debt issuance, as well as heightened uncertainty about the fiscal outlook.

Taking a longer-term perspective of the euro area ten-year OIS rate and its components showed that long-term nominal rates, real rates, rate expectations and term premia had all traded in a relatively narrow range since the fourth quarter of 2022 and were not far above their four-year averages. However, since a trough in late 2024, all components had gradually increased. The bulk of the increase had come after two distinct events: the announcement of the German fiscal package in March 2025 and the start of the Middle East conflict in February 2026. A decomposition of the euro area ten-year nominal OIS rates into structural drivers showed that domestic factors – an improving euro area macroeconomic environment and a reassessment of ECB monetary policy expectations – had been the dominant drivers. US factors seemed to have played some role recently, but spillovers from US to euro area yields had generally been more modest over the past two years. Whereas US term premium shocks had previously explained the largest part of the variation in euro area term premia, this share was estimated to have fallen to 20%. One possible explanation for the structurally weaker spillovers was that upward movements in US term premia could increasingly reflect US-specific factors.

Euro area sovereign bond markets had remained orderly. Sovereign bond spreads over OIS rates had been broadly stable since the Governing Council's previous monetary policy meeting. This suggested that the recent increase in euro area yields had not triggered a broader reassessment of sovereign credit risk, while markets continued to differentiate among issuers.

Regarding exchange rates, the coordinated intervention by the US and Japanese authorities to support the yen had led to an initial sharp appreciation of the Japanese currency against the US dollar, while the euro had appreciated against the US dollar.

On the back of continued positive data surprises on the macroeconomy, strong corporate earnings growth expectations and sustained optimism about artificial intelligence (AI), euro area equity markets had risen further. At the same time, concerns were rising about the increased leverage of AI companies, a significant part of which was off-balance sheet. While direct euro area exposures to AI-related leverage remained limited, investors were increasingly exposed to AI-related valuations and earnings expectations through equity markets. An important question was whether the AI investment boom, and the increase in debt in particular, could generate crowding-out effects in euro area bond markets. So far, euro area markets had absorbed the greater issuance by US hyperscalers without there being a noticeable deterioration in financing conditions for other issuers.

Ms Schnabel concluded by pointing out that euro area financial conditions had tightened modestly since the Governing Council's previous monetary policy meeting. This had been driven by somewhat higher long-term nominal and real rates, as well as an appreciation of the euro, which had been only partly offset by the easing stemming from risk assets.

sections.part: 1. Review of financial, economic and monetary developments and policy options
sections.heading: The global environment and economic and monetary developments in the euro area
paragraphs: Mr Lane then went through the latest economic, monetary and financial developments in the global economy and the euro area. He noted that, six months on, the energy shock triggered by the conflict in the Middle East was generating persistent inflation pressures. After some volatility during the summer, there was renewed upward pressure on oil prices, compounded by an upward shift in refining margins. In addition, spot and forward prices for gas had surged. Oil prices stood at USD 97 per barrel – up 3% since the Governing Council’s July monetary policy meeting – and European diesel crack spreads (i.e. the differences between wholesale petroleum product prices and crude oil prices, often used to estimate refining margins) were above USD 70 per barrel – more than three times their pre-war level. Gas prices stood at €73 per MWh – 17% higher than at the time of the July meeting.

Headline inflation in the euro area, as measured by the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP), had increased to 3.3% in August, from 2.9% in July, according to Eurostat’s flash estimate. Similarly, energy price inflation had risen to 14.3%, after 10.3% in July. This increase was likely to have reflected a strong contribution from refining margins on liquid fuels, as well as higher energy commodity prices. According to the flash estimate, food price inflation had remained unchanged at 1.2%.

So far, indirect effects remained contained, with no material signs of second-round effects. Compensation per employee had grown at an annual rate of 3.3% in the second quarter, down from 3.5% in the first quarter. Rising labour productivity had also helped contain growth in unit labour costs, which had slowed to 2.6%, from 3.5% in the first quarter. At the same time, the more limited growth in unit labour costs had been offset by stronger growth in unit profits, which had risen from 0.3% to 2.2%. Profit margin indicators based on Purchasing Managers’ Indices (PMIs) had remained squeezed in the first two months of the third quarter, although less so than in the second quarter. Negotiated wage growth had continued to ease in the second quarter, to 2.4%. This outcome was broadly in line with the ECB’s wage tracker. This suggested a broadly unchanged outlook for wages since the Governing Council’s previous meeting and pointed to a modest uptick, to 2.7%, in negotiated wage growth in the first half of 2027. Most measures of underlying inflation had been broadly stable in July. At the same time, the lagged effects of the energy shock were expected to continue to exert some pressure on non-energy inflation over the coming year.

The conflict in the Middle East and recent developments in Russia’s unjustified war against Ukraine had pushed the path of energy prices up further. This was likely to keep headline inflation well above target into the first half of 2027. Thereafter, energy inflation should decline and turn negative up to mid-2028, bringing headline inflation down. The baseline of the September ECB staff projections saw headline inflation averaging 3.0% in 2026, 2.5% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028. Compared with the June staff projections, headline inflation had been revised up by 0.2 percentage points for 2027 and by 0.1 percentage points for 2028. The projected headline inflation rate for 2028 would have been 1.9% without the impact of the EU Emissions Trading System 2. Higher energy prices were expected to feed through gradually to core and food price inflation. The improved economic outlook should also contribute to slightly higher core inflation, which was expected to keep rising until early 2027 and stay elevated for the rest of the year, before moderating in 2028. For inflation excluding energy and food, the baseline foresaw 2.5% in 2026, 2.6% in 2027 and 2.3% in 2028.

Inflation expectations over shorter horizons remained at elevated levels, but most measures of longer-term inflation expectations stood at around 2%, supporting the stabilisation of inflation around target in the medium term.

The global economy was expected to strengthen in the near term following a deceleration in the second quarter. Survey indicators suggested a pick-up in global growth momentum in the third quarter, with AI-related investment continuing to be a key driver. Strong trade dynamics in technology products would also continue to support growth in global trade in the near term. Energy supply shortages had eased in recent months, although the PMI scores indicated increasing global supply shortages for semiconductors. Since the previous meeting of the Governing Council, the euro had appreciated by 1.9% against the US dollar and by 0.7% in nominal effective terms.

The euro area economy had proved to be resilient in the second quarter, despite headwinds from the energy shock. Concerns at the start of the Middle East conflict regarding shortages of fertilisers and supply bottlenecks had largely not materialised. Growth was broad-based across countries and sectors. This pattern was likely to have continued into the third quarter. Survey indicators had improved further in the third quarter, with the August PMIs for flash composite output and new orders having edged up compared with July. Manufacturing continued to perform solidly as governments spent more on defence and infrastructure. Consumer confidence had rebounded from low levels, helping services recover from the initial energy shock. Increased AI-related activity was visible in digital services, business investment and exports.

The labour market had remained robust, with the unemployment rate unchanged in July at 6.4%. Growth in employment and the labour force continued to slow, while productivity had gradually picked up. Labour demand had cooled further, as the job vacancy rate had edged down by 0.1 percentage points to 2.1% in the second quarter, and Indeed job postings had weakened, albeit less markedly than in previous months.

With respect to fiscal policies, the September staff projections were broadly unchanged from the June projections, foreseeing the euro area budget deficit to increase from 3.0% of GDP in 2025 to 3.6% in 2026 and 3.7% in 2027, before moderating again slightly to 3.6% in 2028. The projection for the fiscal stance, defined as the change in the cyclically adjusted primary balance, indicated a substantial fiscal loosening by 0.5 percentage points in 2026, which would support the economy. This loosening would, however, be reversed in 2027 and 2028, constituting a headwind to growth in those years.

Looking ahead, the near-term growth outlook had improved compared with the last round of staff projections, reflecting, in particular, the resilience of private consumption and public spending. Over the medium term, consumption should be supported by gradually falling energy prices and a strong labour market. Growth would increasingly be bolstered by business and housing investment. Export growth should benefit from rising foreign demand but was being held back by competitiveness challenges and uncertainty about global trade policies. The September ECB staff baseline projection for economic growth was 0.9% for 2026, 1.4% for 2027 and 1.5% for 2028. This was an upward revision for both 2026 and 2027, mainly reflecting the greater than expected resilience of the euro area economy.

The outlook remained highly uncertain and critically dependent on geopolitical developments. Risks were to the upside for inflation and to the downside for economic growth. In relation to the energy shock, the updated scenarios put together by ECB staff illustrated the broad range of outcomes for how growth and inflation would evolve under different assumptions about its intensity and duration, as well as its indirect and second-round effects. The September projections baseline was complemented with a milder scenario, an adverse scenario and a severe scenario, calibrated using market‑implied probability distributions for commodity prices from the fourth quarter of 2026 onwards. Under the adverse and severe scenarios, inflation would remain above target over the entire projection horizon, while growth would be lower than in the baseline. Under the milder scenario, inflation would moderate more quickly than in the baseline and fall below target in the medium term, while growth would be slightly above the baseline for 2027 and 2028.

Market interest rates had increased since the Governing Council’s previous meeting, reflecting similar moves in global markets. Financing costs were adjusting smoothly to the increase in ECB interest rates in June: bank lending rates for firms had risen, to stand at 3.8% in June and July, from 3.6% in May. The cost of market-based corporate debt had stood at 4.0% in July, which was similar to previous months and well above its level before the conflict in the Middle East. The annual growth rate of bank lending to firms, which usually responded to changes in monetary policy with a longer delay, had increased further to 4.4% in July, from 4.0% in May and June. The annual growth rate of corporate bond issuance had been 3.4%, after 3.6% in June and 3.3% in May. Mortgage rates had been unchanged in June and July, at 3.5%, while mortgage lending growth had softened to 3.0% in July, from 3.1% in May and June.
